newsitem.title: USA: Rain boosts U.S. Northwest hydroelectric output.
newsitem.headline: Rain boosts U.S. Northwest hydroelectric output.

text.p: Recent heavy rain in the U.S. Pacific Northwest continues to boost hydroelectric power generation, but demand is also higher due to the colder weather, industry sources said Wednesday.
Up to 10 inches of heavy, wet snow fell in the Seattle area on Tuesday, while Portland and other parts of Oregon were hit hard with rain.

Bonneville Power Administration, which markets power produced at federal dams in the Northwest, on Wednesday offered 600 megawatts of surplus next-day power, up from 400 MW on Tuesday and 200 MW on Monday.
The agency has also raised offer prices for the power by $5.75 per megawatt hour since Monday.
"There is some activity at projects on the Willamette River," said Cindy Hendrickson, chief of the agency's reservoir control center in Portland, Ore.
"The 11 projects on the Willamette started at virtually empty, as they should be at this time of year, but as of this morning they are 30 to 40 percent full."

She noted that several hydroelectric dams on the Columbia River have been readied for possible flood control needs, including making room in the reservoirs at the John Day and Grand Coulee dams for the rising water.
Power generation "is slightly increased by the higher flows on the Columbia," Hendrickson noted. "Bonneville Dam is running at full power, but it is all being used."
She said the current high flows will probably peak late Thursday or early Friday, when less intense rain is forecast to fall on the region.
